case_name: R. A. S. v. Re. L.
text:
JG1793

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-12-269238-030

DATE:

MAY 7, 2004

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF THE HONOURABLE
CLÉMENT GASCON, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

R. A. S.

Plaintiff

v.

RE. L.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT
RENDERED ORALLY

ON MOTIONS FOR
PROVISIONAL MEASURES

______________________________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

On provisional measures, I believe that it is
more important to render a timely and rapid judgment than a well written or
well substantiated one.  Thus, the reason why I render my judgment orally
immediately rather than in writing at a later date.

[
2
]

I will provide explanations for my findings and
conclusions, realizing full well that an oral judgment does not have the
structure and perhaps the prose of a written one. I apologize in advance to the
parties and their learned counsels for any mistakes of that nature.

[
3
]

Pursuant to the Motions for provisional measures
made by both parents, I have to decide mainly three issues here:

1.

Whether the children, Am. and F., should be the
subject of a joint physical custody or of an exclusive one of the mother, with
extended access rights to the father;

2.

Whether the former common domicile of the
spouses should be sold immediately;

3.

What, based on the findings on the first two
issues, should be the amount of the child and spousal support to be paid under
the circumstances.

[
4
]

These are the main issues.  There will remain at
the end some secondary ones pertaining to a number of smaller points:  the
claim of the father for the return of some files, the cease and desist request
of the father on harassment allegations by the mother, and the claim of the
mother for the reimbursement of the Florida trip of December 2002.

[
5
]

I will address all of these in the conclusions
of my judgment in order to try to provide clearer guidelines for the parties in
the future.  This entails a very detailed set of conclusions indeed.  Suffice
to say at this point that I believe the parties will never be able to go to the
next step and put their relationship behind them unless they start right now to
be more reasonable in their respective behaviour towards one another.

[
6
]

No matter what they may think, even if they are
not a couple anymore, they will remain the parents of Am. and F. for all their
life and they are condemned to interact together because of that.  Each of the
parents has the benefit of very able and learned counsels and I trust they will
listen to their sound advices to approach their conflict in a more positive and
responsible manner in the future.

[
7
]

That said, my role here is to decide where the
parties have failed to agree and I now address the various questions at issue.

THE
CHILDREN CUSTODY

[
8
]

Each judge brings to a custody hearing his or
her own personal views and experience.  I am no different.  Being a parent and
a father myself, I confess from the start that I am a strong believer in the
equal sharing of the responsibilities and benefits of parenthood between the
father and the mother.

[
9
]

Therefore, I tend to favour a joint custody when
the applicable criteria are met.  I am of the view that joint custody should
always be seriously considered when the parental capacities of the parents are
present, when they are ready to devote the necessary time and energy, and when
there are no physical, psychological, geographical or educational counter
indications.

[
10
]

Here, many points favour a joint custody for Am.
and F..  To name a few:

-

Both parents are undoubtedly good and competent;

-

There are no counter indications from proximity
or educational standpoints;

-

The father is devoted, ready to invest in his
children and interested to do so.  He wants to be part of their life.  For
instance, he drives them to school every morning and not many would do so
considering the distances he must travel to do it.  He calls them daily and
again, not everyone would do so. He has made the necessary arrangements to
accommodate them at his duplex in A.  He already spends 50% of the holiday time
with the children.  He is finally quite reasonable in the transition that he
proposes for the change to a joint custody that he advocates.

[
11
]

However, notwithstanding all of these, I come to
the conclusion that at this point in time, a joint custody should not be
implemented immediately for the following reasons.

[
12
]

There is a major, and I stress major,
communication problem between the parties that cannot be ignored.  There is, I
believe, a serious lack of trust and respect on the part of both, and I insist
both, parents.  There is also a serious lack of flexibility between them with
their present arrangement.  It is serious enough to suggest that there is a
strong need for improvement.

[
13
]

I do not mean by that that one parent can block,
simply because of difficulties of communication, a joint custody by not
cooperating. However here, it is an important factor that militates against
it.

[
14
]

But under the circumstances, that is not all.
There is more.

[
15
]

I believe some stability is required for the
children considering what happened over the last three years.  The mother has
been the principal caregiver of the children over the years and in both
separations lived by the parties so far, there has never been a joint custody
arrangement.  Simply put, the children have never experienced it. The status
quo of their present situation will allow a better stability than the change to
a joint custody would.

[
16
]

In addition, there is in my view a valid concern
for the heavy business travel schedule of the father.  Even though I note his
willingness to adjust, I have not heard any evidence as to how he would cope
with the weeks or days where he is not present because of these travel
commitments.

[
17
]

Lastly, but by far not the least important,
here, the children wishes have been expressed clearly.  It is the understanding
of both parties that the children are happy with the present situation and
would prefer a status quo.  Their views are not decisive but they are
noteworthy, as they are respectively aged 10 and 12.

[
18
]

From a review of these criteria, I conclude that
we can easily distinguish the decisions cited by Me Nantel.

[
19
]

The first and fourth decisions in her book of
authorities dealt with matters where a report of an expert recommended a joint
custody.

[
20
]

In the sixth decision she cited, the children
wanted the joint custody.

[
21
]

In the second decision she referred to, the
child was only 21 months and no view was expressed on his part.

[
22
]

In the fifth decision she cited, the mother did
not favour any contact with the father.

[
23
]

Finally, in the third decision she submitted,
whatever was called the "status quo" was basically a three weeks
period.

[
24
]

I am not saying that it may not come to a joint
custody situation at the accessory measures level.  Indeed, I believe it may
well come to that at some point, as the father is entitled to his children as
much as the mother.  But maybe later, not now.  I do not think that the parties
are ready for it presently, nor do I think it is time to make experiments at
the provisional level.

[
25
]

Therefore, as far as the custody is concerned, I
conclude that the physical custody will remain with the mother, with the same
every second weekend access rights to the father, the sharing 50-50 of all the
holidays, the same entitlement of the father to the daily phone calls with his
children and the same entitlement of the father to drive his children to
school.

[
26
]

In addition, I am ready to make some progress
towards a more equal sharing of the parental time between the father and the
mother.  Therefore, I will give additional access rights to the father for the
night following the Wednesday dinner if he wants it.

[
27
]

Finally, for sake of clarity, my conclusions
will also repeat that the legal custody remains joint and that decisions on the
children are those of both parents, not only those of the mother.

THE SALE
OF THE COMMON DOMICILE

[
28
]

The father wants the immediate sale of the
common domicile because he says he cannot afford it.

[
29
]

In all due respect, the father has not proven
this.  From the evidence heard, I do not believe he cannot afford it.  The real
numbers do not support that allegation.  The revised Form III and Statement of
income that are included as part of Annex A, B and C of my conclusions show it.

[
30
]

Furthermore, I do not see the urgency to sell
that house right now.  The mother makes a strong argument that she will try to
keep it on the merits; she wants to retain it for the children.  She should at
least be afforded the opportunity to present and make her claim at the
accessory measures as she alleges in her cross-demand of August 11, 2003.

[
31
]

Notably when one realizes that in this case,
thanks to the efforts of the attorneys on both sides, the two Rule 15 have been
filed in December 2003 and in all likelihood, the matter should be heard on the
merits within approximately a year.

[
32
]

Again, the decisions cited by Me Nantel in this
respect should be distinguished.

[
33
]

In the seventh decision of her book of
authorities, the mother was slowing the Court process and there was an utmost
necessity to sell the house.

[
34
]

In the eighth decision of her book of
authorities, the revenues of the parties had decreased and they had simply no
means to keep the house.  Here, to the contrary, the revenues of the parties
have increased over the last twelve months.

[
35
]

In the ninth decision, the mother had agreed to
sell the house.

[
36
]

Finally, in the tenth decision, the father had
to live at his parent's place because he did not have the means to even pay for
an apartment for himself.

[
37
]

All of these are quite different from our
situation.

[
38
]

In short, the father has not established the
immediate need to sell the house at the provisional stage.  He had the burden
to convince, which he has not met.

THE CHILD
AND SPOUSAL SUPPORT

[
39
]

I now deal with the child and spousal support.

[
40
]

The first step in establishing the relevant amounts
is to determine the revenues of the father and the mother based on the evidence
heard.  I need to do so for 2003 and 2004, as both years are relevant: the
Motion of the mother claiming support is dated August 11, 2003 and any judgment
will be retroactive to that date.

[
41
]

For the father, I believe the numbers are
obvious.  For 2003, his income tax return indicates a revenue of $216,617 and
this number will be the one I retain. For 2004, it is also easy.  At a minimum,
his salary and bonus will stand at $236,000 based on the evidence.

[
42
]

The mother says it should be higher due to some
non-taxable benefits.  I disagree.  The evidence to that end is contradictory.
The mother says they exist, while the father denies it for the most part.
There has been no convincing evidence presented that would lead me to believe
that the amounts are higher, even by merely $5,000 or $10,000 as suggested by
the mother's attorney.  I am reluctant to fix revenues by simply guessing and I
will not do so.

[
43
]

I do appreciate that the father has not be
forthright on his revenues for 2003 and 2004.  I consider it difficult to
accept that when he signed the sworn affidavits on his revenues, he did not
realize that for 2003, he had excluded the $31,000 bonus he had received, and
that for 2004, he had excluded the $68,000 bonus he was paid a few weeks
before.  The father will suffer the consequences of these
"oversights" in the calculations that will be made to fix the child
support.  However, that is not sufficient in itself to put aside his testimony
on the non-taxable benefits he says he did not receive.

[
44
]

On this point, the burden was that of the mother
who alleged it and she has not met it.

[
45
]

For the revenues of the mother, 2003 is easy.
From her income tax return, it stands at $53,464.  For 2004, it is more
complicated, but I conclude it should stand at $46,240 for the following
reasons.

[
46
]

The evidence established that she first received
four months of revenue from January to April at an annual salary of $40,500,
namely $13,500 for these months.  Second, from April to August, she will be
receiving four months at an annual gross salary of $44,161 or $32,436 net,
which represents another $14,720.  Third, I believe that on the balance of
probabilities, she should return to work in September and therefore, I
calculated the last four months of the year at $54,060 annually, or $18,020 for
this period.

[
47
]

The total of these three sums stands at
$46,240.  Based on the evidence, that number is the closest to the reality for
the year 2004.

[
48
]

That done, for the calculation of the child
support, I simply need to apply these numbers to three different sets of Child
Support Determination Forms.  They are attached as Annex A, B and C to my
conclusions.

[
49
]

Annex A is for the year 2003, where I used a
figure of 106 days for the father's access rights.  Annex B is for the first
five months of 2004, again using 106 days for the father's access rights.
Annex C is for the balance of 2004, using 124 days for the father's access
rights.

[
50
]

I calculated the number of days for the father's
access rights as follows.

[
51
]

I considered that there were 14 weeks shared at
50%, namely 9 weeks in the summer, 2 weeks at Christmas, 1 week at school
break, 1 week at Passover and 1 week of Jewish holidays, for a total of 49
days.

[
52
]

For the remaining 38 weeks, I calculated the
father's access rights at 2 days and 2/3 times 19 weeks, namely 1 weekend every
2 weeks, plus 4 hours for the Wednesday dinner and evening during 38 weeks.
All these total 106 days.

[
53
]

As I will give to the father, starting June 1
st
,
the entitlement to spend a full evening and night with the children on
Wednesdays, it adds another 18 days or so to the balance of 2004, hence the
different number of days (124) in Annex C.

[
54
]

In addition, to calculate the child support, I
need to evaluate the special needs of the children.  There is an issue here as
to what we should do with the school tuitions of $12,000 that the father pays
directly to third parties.  This is the decision of the parties and I cannot
redo the history for 2003 and 2004.  They chose that manner of doing and they
will have to live with it.

[
55
]

Notwithstanding, in making the calculations of
the child support to be paid, I need to adjust the figures, since excluding
this $12,000 from the calculation forms would entail the mother not paying for
her share of these tuition fees.  Based on the revenues of the parties, her
share of that amount should be roughly 17% or 18%.  I have attached the
relevant forms to my conclusions and they indeed show the impact.  Therefore, I
will take that into consideration in establishing the applicable numbers.

[
56
]

For the other special costs, I believe they
should be limited to $1,000 to account for the dance lessons, some of the
uniforms and some skiing lessons.  I do not think the evidence is clear as to
what exactly that figure should be, but it is definitely closer to $1,000 than
$2,000.

[
57
]

The figures I arrived at for the child support,
and again the forms show it, indicate consequently the following:

-

For 2003, namely from August to December, a
child support of $1,232.20 monthly;

-

For the first five months of 2004, a child
support of $1,370.81 monthly;

-

Starting June 2004, an amount of $1,282.89
monthly.

[
58
]

These are owed by the father to the mother for
the children.

[
59
]

As they concern the child support payments, I do
not have any discretion to reduce them and they should not be reduced.  I
realize it is much higher than what the father expected, but this is due to the
fact that his real revenues are much higher than what he divulged.  My
conclusions will provide for some payment terms, but not very extended as these
are for the benefit of the children.

[
60
]

On the issue of the house expenses, let me say
right now that if they have any impact here, it is on the spousal support
numbers, not on the child support ones.  I do not believe that they should
reduce the amount of the child support payments.

[
61
]

The attorney for Mr. S. has made an argument to
that end, but I do not have any basis to reassess the "lodging
component" of the basic need number of the formulas.  First, I am not
convinced by the evidence submitted in this respect and second, I believe it is
a false problem.

[
62
]

If the house expenses were being paid half and
half by the parties as joint owners, this would increase the expenses of the
mother and decrease those of the father.  It would change the picture of their
means and needs for spousal support, but it would not impact upon the child
support figures.

[
63
]

I turn now to the spousal support.

[
64
]

If the numbers for child support are high, it is
a different story for the spousal support.  On this issue, the main points to
consider at the provisional stage are the means and needs of the parties,
remembering that my judgment will basically have an impact for approximately a
year or so.

[
65
]

Again the scenarios that I have calculated are
part of Annex A, B and C to my conclusions and the detailed calculations are
included therein.  The revenues are known and the expenses have been reviewed.

[
66
]

To get the real picture of the needs of the
mother, I excluded from her expenses all the ones relating to the house which
the father pays and will continue to pay as the house is not to be sold for the
time being.  Again, the parties agreed to that manner of doing at the interim
level and I cannot redo the history, at least not at this stage.

[
67
]

In calculating the expenses of the mother, I
have also reduced many of the numbers that I consider too high or which go
beyond her own needs.  For instance, I have reduced the amounts for the phone,
for the cable, for the repairs and for the vacations.  I have excluded the
amounts for the summer camps as no evidence supports it.  I have excluded the
amounts for the lawyer's fees in 2003 and only considered it in 2004, as I
would otherwise count it twice.  I have finally reduced other numbers that I
consider were duplicating in part the components of the child support
payments.

[
68
]

I will not repeat the figures here because they
are part of Annex A, B and C and the parties will be provided with those.  I
note however that the numbers I arrived at for 2003 indicate that when the
house expenses are paid by the father and when one factors into account the
child support that will be paid, the mother suffers no deficit in 2003.  For
2004, any deficit is minimal.

[
69
]

As for the father, in looking at his expenses, I
basically left them as is, except for three elements that I have excluded.  The
$5,000 for summer camps which has not been established, the $150 for the mother
which is the object of the calculation that has to be made, and the $100 for
the third party which I believe should only come after the needs of the
children and the wife have been fully met.

[
70
]

Again, when I look at these figures, for 2003, I
arrive at a very small deficit of less than $100 for the father.  For 2004, I
even arrive at a surplus considering these revised expenses.

[
71
]

Based on these analysis which the parties will
have with the conclusions, and considering the child support that will be paid,
it is my view that there is no need to add any spousal support for 2003 over
and above the expenses paid by the father for the common domicile which stand
at $2,644 per month.

[
72
]

Indeed, it is appropriate, and my conclusions
will say so, to specify that nothing further is owed by the father with respect
to the $150 agreed to on an interim basis. When one adds the child support
payments to the common domicile expenses paid, the needs of the mother are
fully met at least up to the date of this judgment.

[
73
]

For the balance of 2004, there is a very small
need for the mother, which the father by the way has the means to fulfill.
However, for the following reasons, I decide not to grant additional spousal
support over and above the payment by the father of the common domicile
expenses and the child support.

[
74
]

First, the difference is minimal and if there is
a deficit in 2004, it is amply compensated by the excess calculated for 2003.

[
75
]

Second, there will be important arrears of child
support to be paid by the father.  I come to a figure of some $5,544 for 2003
and $6,854 for 2004 when one considers that these are retroactive.  This will
be paid to the mother and she will basically end up receiving all that she
would have been entitled to for those two years.  As a result, I do not want to
jeopardize any of these child support payments by adding other spousal support
payments of a minimal impact.

[
76
]

Third, as we will see, over and above the child
support payments, it is my conclusion that the father will have to reimburse to
the mother the cost of the trip to Florida in 2002, which also adds to his
burden.

[
77
]

Finally, in assessing the needs of the mother, I
cannot ignore the fact that her balance sheet is very good, considering the
estate of her late mother which I value at some $115,000 at the minimum.  I do
not believe she will suffer at all from that standpoint between now and the
hearing on the accessory measures.

[
78
]

The overall picture therefore indicates that it
is fair to conclude like that and to leave the situation of the spousal support
as such.

THE OTHER
ISSUES

[
79
]

There remains only the secondary issues to deal
with.

[
80
]

I already said what my decision is on the
Florida trip of December 2002.  On the balance of probabilities, the evidence
establishes that the father agreed to reimburse the mother for that expense
from his bonus of 2003, which stood at $31,000.  He did not.  The mother
affirms it, while the father denies it in part, but not entirely. He did indeed
reimburse $1,000 of it.  The testimony of the mother is more credible on that
point.

[
81
]

As to the value of that trip, I disagree with
the amounts given to me by the attorneys.  From the amounts underlined in
yellow in Exhibits U-10 and D-7, the numbers rather stand at $5,698.21 for U-10
and $747.93 for D-7, for a total of $6,446.04.  Deducting the $1,000 already
paid by the father, the balance owed stands at $5,446.04.  I believe it is
reasonable to allow a 90 days delay for the father to repay this amount under
the circumstances.

[
82
]

Finally, to avoid further problems, I believe it
is appropriate to provide, in my conclusions, for the return of the father's files
that the mother may still have in her possession, if any.  I believe it is also
appropriate to remind the parties to stop any harassment and not to criticize
and denigrate each other in front of the children.

[
83
]

I do hope that these reasons and conclusions
will assist the parties in moving forward with their relationship as parents in
a constructive manner.  I sincerely wish them good luck for the future, which,
I remind them, remains in their hands and not in those of the Court.

[
84
]

For the record, I will now read the conclusions
of my judgment.  As I indicated early on, I remit to the attorneys a copy of
these conclusions, as well as a copy of Annex A, B and C from which the various
numbers have been calculated.

[
85
]

FOR THE REASONS GIVEN ORALLY AND REGISTERED,
THE COURT
:

[
86
]

GRANTS
joint
legal custody of the minor children Am. and F. to the mother and the father;

[
87
]

DECLARES
that the
parents shall continue to exercise jointly the parental authority over their
children and
ORDERS
them to consult each other before taking any
decision on an important issue affecting the children, notably on matters
pertaining to education, health, summer camps and extra-curricular activities;

[
88
]

GRANTS
to the
mother the physical custody of the children who shall reside principally with
her;

[
89
]

GRANTS
to the
father the following prolonged visiting and outing rights of the children and
ORDERS

the mother to respect such:

-

Every second weekend
from Friday after school or late afternoon until Monday morning,
commencing immediately.  In the event the Monday of a weekend access is a
holiday, the father will have the children until the Tuesday morning;

-

Every Wednesday

after school or late afternoon until the following Thursday morning, commencing
with the beginning of June 2004;

-

Every morning
,
the father shall continue to drive the children to school;

-

For all the holidays period
, including the religious, legal or school holidays, the father
shall have the children 50% of the time, on a schedule to be mutually agreed
upon by the parties;

-

For the summer holidays
of the children, and beginning with the first full week thereof,
the children shall be with the father and the mother on an alternate week
schedule arrangement, from Friday late afternoon to the following Friday late
afternoon;

-

Finally, the father shall be entitled to
continue to talk on the phone with the children once during the evening of
every week-day of the school year;

[
90
]

GRANTS
to the
mother the continued exclusive use of the former common domicile, to the
exclusion of the father.  Notwithstanding, the mother shall leave a set of the
house keys with Ra. and T. L. in the event of any emergencies which may arise;

[
91
]

ORDERS
the mother
and the father not to denigrate or criticize the conduct and behaviour of each
other in front of the children and not to discuss their pending divorce
proceedings with or in front of the children;

[
92
]

ORDERS
the mother
and the father not to harass each other and not to contact or communicate with
the employer of the other or the employees of these employers, save for their
own personal friends;

[
93
]

ORDERS
the mother
to return to the father, within seven days of the date of this judgment, any
files or personal belongings of the father still in her possession or still in
the former common domicile;

[
94
]

ORDERS
the father
to continue to pay directly to the third parties creditors the schooling
expenses, including the tuition fees, the summer camps and the RESP of the
children;

[
95
]

ORDERS
the father
to pay to the mother, as child support payments for Am. and F., the following
amounts which take into consideration the above payments of the father to third
parties creditors (the Child Support Determination Forms used are attached as
Annex A, B, and C):

-

From the date of service of the mother's Motion
for provisional measures, namely August 11, 2003, to December 31, 2003, a
monthly alimony of $1,232.20 ($14,786 on an annual basis), the whole within 30
days of the date of this judgment;

-

From January 1st, 2004 to May 31st, 2004, a
monthly alimony of $1,370.81 ($16,449.67 on an annual basis), the whole within
60 days of the date of this judgment;

-

From June 1st, 2004 forward, a monthly alimony
of $1,282.89 ($15,514.63 on an annual basis). This alimony shall be paid
directly by the father to the mother by equal instalments on the 1st and 15th
of each month up until the Minister of Revenue advises him otherwise and begins
collecting these child support payments;

[
96
]

ORDERS
the father
to continue to pay directly to the third parties creditors the following
monthly expenses pertaining to the former common domicile, namely the mortgage,
the taxes, the electricity and the home insurance;

[
97
]

DECLARES
that in
view of the above payments of the father to third parties creditors, the father
does not have to pay to the mother additional spousal support payments at this
stage, including any outstanding balance owed, if any, pursuant to paragraph 9
of the Consent Agreement of June 17, 2003 (the applicable Form III and
Statement of Income used are attached as part of Annex A, B, and C);

[
98
]

ORDERS
the father
to reimburse to the mother the sum of $5,446.04 for the balance of the cost of
the Florida trip of December 2002 of the parties, the whole within 90 days of
the date of this judgment;

[
99
]

WITHOUT

COSTS
.

CLÉMENT
GASCON, J.S.C.

Me
Francine Nantel

Robinson Sheppard Shapiro

Attorneys
for Plaintiff

Me
Asher Neudorfer

Sarna
Neudorfer

Attorneys
for Defendant

Date
of hearing:

MAY
4, 5 and 6, 2004.

Reasons transcribed and revised on June
11, 2004.
